title: Respond to a cease-and-desist
summary: A cease-and-desist is a demand, not a court order, but ignoring one is how lawsuits start. Note what they are claiming and the deadline in the letter. There is no statutory response deadline; the letter, and any lawsuit that follows, sets the pace. Preserve your evidence before anything changes. Get IP counsel involved before you reply, admit anything, or sign anything. Your options are three: comply (stop or rebrand), negotiate (coexistence or license), or contest. Educational guidance, not legal advice. The active work is a few founder-hours; the other side's reply time is out of your hands.

parts.title: Read the letter calmly: who sent it, the exact claims, and its stated response deadline

execution.rationale: Read the supplied letter and extract its sender, actual claims and stated deadline without deciding the legal response.

parts.title: Preserve the evidence: archive the letter, your first-use dates, sales records, and screenshots

execution.rationale: Archive the supplied letter, first-use records and screenshots as a local evidence set without altering originals.

parts.title: Look up the claimed mark on the trademark register the letter relies on: registration status, goods and services, filing dates

parts.title: Choose counsel for the response (IP/trademark litigation)

execution.rationale: Compare the listed counsel's documented litigation scope and experience for the company's engagement decision.
The authorized client personally signs counsel's engagement through an unspecified execution method.

parts.title: Assess with counsel: their mark's strength, your actual use, and the options — comply, negotiate, or contest

execution.rationale: Counsel and the client assess the claimed mark and actual use, then choose a response. The consultation medium is unspecified.

parts.title: Draft the response (or the rebrand/coexistence plan counsel recommends)

execution.rationale: Draft the response or alternative plan from counsel's selected strategy and supplied supporting evidence.

parts.title: Send the response before the letter's stated deadline

execution.rationale: The permitted response channel and actual deadline depend on the letter and counsel's instructions.

parts.title: Wait for the counterparty's reply and calendar the follow-through

execution.rationale: The counterparty supplies the reply; monitoring and calendaring do not perform that response.

metadata.trigger: A cease-and-desist letter claiming trademark or IP infringement arrives by mail or email.
metadata.supportReason: Assessing the exposure, choosing the strategy, and writing the response letter are work for counsel and the founder; that is legal judgment, not API calls. An agent can preserve the evidence file and pull the claimed mark's register record; it cannot answer a legal demand for you.

geoNotes.summary: A C&D usually arrives as a letter before claim under the IP pre-action regime — and the UK's unjustified-threats rules (Intellectual Property (Unjustified Threats) Act 2017) cut both ways: a groundless infringement threat can itself be actionable, which disciplines both the letter you received and any reply you send. IP counsel before answering, same as the US flow.

The German form is the Abmahnung with a strafbewehrte Unterlassungserklärung attached: signing that cease-and-desist declaration creates a contract with penalties for every future breach, so never sign it unreviewed. Short stated deadlines are normal and an einstweilige Verfügung (preliminary injunction) can follow quickly — counsel first.

A mise en demeure letter typically precedes a contrefaçon action; preserve your evidence and answer through IP counsel — once litigation starts, saisie-contrefaçon evidence seizures move quickly, so the calm, reasoned reply matters as much as in the US.

A C&D under the Trade Marks Act 1999 works like the US letter — and Section 142 provides a remedy against groundless threats, which a reasoned reply can invoke. Pull the claimed mark's record on the registry before answering, with counsel.

The letter arrives as a carta de interpelação before an infringement action in the specialised IP court — capture its own stated deadline, verify the sender's INPI registrations, and answer through counsel; never ignore it.

Canadian C&Ds work like US ones — a demand with its own deadline, not an order, and no unjustified-threats statute tempers them — so verify the sender's CIPO registrations and respond through counsel before the stated date.

A C&D usually lands as a letter of demand, and Singapore's IP statutes carry groundless-threat provisions (Trade Marks Act 1998 s 35) that cut both ways — an overreaching infringement threat is itself actionable, so route the response through counsel.

A C&D usually arrives as a letter of demand, and Australian IP statutes carry unjustified-threats actions (trade marks, patents, designs), so a groundless infringement threat can itself be actionable — get IP counsel before answering, same as the US flow.
